questions.question: What does the prefix 'quasi' mean in the context of quasi-experimental research?

answers.text: Resembling
Almost
Partial
Incomplete

questions.question: What is the primary characteristic that distinguishes quasi-experimental research from true experimental research?

answers.text: Quasi-experiments lack random assignment to conditions or counterbalancing
Quasi-experiments do not manipulate an independent variable
Quasi-experiments cannot be conducted in laboratory settings
Quasi-experiments always use within-subjects designs

questions.question: In terms of internal validity, where do quasi-experiments generally fall?

answers.text: Between non-experimental studies and true experiments
Higher than true experiments
Equal to non-experimental studies
Lower than all other research designs

questions.question: What major problem does quasi-experimental research eliminate compared to non-experimental research?

answers.text: The directionality problem
The problem of confounding variables
The problem of demand characteristics
The problem of low external validity

questions.question: What is the major limitation of the one-group posttest only design?

answers.text: The lack of a control or comparison group
The inability to manipulate the independent variable
The requirement for random assignment
The excessive time required to complete the study

questions.question: In a one-group pretest-posttest design, what threat to internal validity refers to events that occur between the pretest and posttest?

answers.text: History
Maturation
Testing
Instrumentation

questions.question: What term describes the threat to internal validity when participants change naturally over time due to growth and learning?

answers.text: Maturation
History
Regression to the mean
Spontaneous remission

questions.question: What does 'testing' refer to as a threat to internal validity?

answers.text: When measuring the dependent variable during the pretest affects participants' responses at posttest
When the measuring instrument changes over time
When extreme scores move toward the average
When participants improve without treatment

questions.question: What is regression to the mean?

answers.text: The tendency for extreme scores on one occasion to be less extreme on the next occasion
The tendency for measurement instruments to become less reliable over time
The tendency for participants to become fatigued during repeated testing
The tendency for control groups to improve at the same rate as treatment groups

questions.question: According to Posternak and Miller's research, what percentage did participants in waitlist control conditions improve before receiving treatment for depression?
In Hans Eysenck's 1952 article on psychotherapy effectiveness, what proportion of patients improved between pretest and posttest?

answers.text: About two thirds
About one half
About three quarters
About one third

questions.question: What is a time series in the context of interrupted time-series design?

answers.text: A set of measurements taken at intervals over a period of time
A single measurement taken before and after treatment
A comparison between two different groups
A random assignment procedure conducted over time

questions.question: What advantage does the interrupted time-series design have over a simple pretest-posttest design?

answers.text: Multiple measurements help distinguish treatment effects from normal variation
It eliminates the need for a control group
It allows for random assignment of participants
It requires fewer participants

questions.question: What defines a nonequivalent groups design?

answers.text: A between-subjects design in which participants have not been randomly assigned to conditions
A within-subjects design without counterbalancing
A design that does not manipulate an independent variable
A design that uses only posttest measurements

questions.question: What is differential history as a threat to internal validity in nonequivalent groups designs?

answers.text: When something occurs in one group but not the other that affects the outcome
When participants in different groups mature at different rates
When measurement instruments differ between groups
When participants drop out of one group more than the other

questions.question: What is a key strength of the pretest-posttest design with switching replication?

answers.text: It includes a built-in replication across two different samples
It eliminates the need for pretesting
It allows for random assignment of participants
It requires only one measurement occasion

questions.question: In the switching replication with treatment removal design, what happens to the first group when the treatment is added to the second group?

answers.text: The treatment is removed from the first group
The first group continues to receive the treatment
The first group receives a different treatment
The first group is dismissed from the study

questions.question: According to the chapter, which quasi-experimental designs are highest in internal validity?

answers.text: Those that include a switching replication
Those that use only posttest measurements
Those conducted in laboratory settings
Those with the largest sample sizes

questions.question: In the interrupted time-series design with nonequivalent groups, what improvement is made over the basic interrupted time-series design?

answers.text: A control group is added
Random assignment is implemented
More frequent measurements are taken

questions.question: What is spontaneous remission?

answers.text: The tendency for medical and psychological problems to improve over time without treatment
The tendency for participants to drop out of studies over time
The tendency for measurement errors to accumulate over time
The tendency for treatment effects to fade after intervention ends
